A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

maculatin‐1.1 inserts in a predominantly α‐helical conformation into the negatively charged membrane DMPG and that it is the amphipathic character of the peptide, not its charge, which is responsible for this behaviour.

the amphipathicity of the helical structure of maculatin 2.1 is a crucial factor for its insertion and activity in membranes, while the presence of a net negative charge on the peptide is not essential for membrane insertion.
the insertion of the peptide is driven by the amphipathic nature of the peptide and its high concentration on the membrane.
The main takeaway from our work is that
maculatin is a pore‐forming antimicrobial peptide, with the pore‐forming mechanism likely to be the same for both Gram‐positive and Gram‐negative bacteria.
the amphipathicity of the peptide, which is a key factor in its biological function, is not a sufficient condition for membrane insertion and that the peptide structure must be considered as well.

, although the peptide is biologically inactive, the peptide can still insert in a membrane and form a helical structure, which may be important for the peptide to interact with the membrane and form pores.
